title: How Ukrainian works: nouns, gender and cases
objectives: I can name the parts of speech and the main terms of grammar in English and in Ukrainian, such as 'іме́нник', 'прикме́тник', 'відмі́нок' and 'рід'.
I can explain that Ukrainian has no articles and no present-tense word for 'is', and say sentences such as 'Ма́ма тут.' and 'Це кни́га.'
I can tell the gender of most nouns from their ending and make the adjective 'нови́й' agree with a noun.
I can name the seven cases with their questions and say what each one does.
I can ask a yes or no question with 'чи', negate with 'не', and recognize sound changes inside a word such as 'кіт' and 'кота́' or 'кни́га' and 'у кни́зі'.

vocabulary.note: Built on 'ім’я́', name: a noun names a person, place, thing or idea. The plural is 'іме́нники'.
Built on 'прикме́та', a distinguishing feature: an adjective names a feature of a noun and agrees with it. In the example, «» are the Ukrainian quotation marks.

example.source: 'Нова́ кни́га': an adjective and a noun.

vocabulary.note: Built on 'ім’я́', like 'іме́нник': a pronoun stands in for a noun or points at one. The plural is 'займе́нники'.
Built on 'ім’я́' as well: a preposition stands before a noun, and it decides the noun's case.

example.source: 'У кни́зі': a preposition and a noun.

vocabulary.note: A form of a noun that shows its job in the sentence. Built on 'відміня́ти', to change. Other forms drop the 'о', as in the plural 'відмі́нки'.
In grammar, the class a noun belongs to; in everyday speech, a family line. Other forms use the stem 'род-', as in 'ро́ду'.
Built on 'чолові́к', man. Outside grammar it means 'men's' or 'male'.
Built on 'жі́нка', woman. Outside grammar it means 'women's' or 'female'.
Literally 'middle': the neuter is the middle gender, between masculine and feminine. Its stem ends in a soft consonant, so its other forms are 'сере́дня', 'сере́днє', 'сере́дні'.

example.source: Neuter gender: window, life, first name.
example.source_literal: Middle gender: window, life, first name.

vocabulary.note: Built on 'закі́нчити', to finish. Neuter, because it ends in '-я' after the doubled 'нн'. The plural has the same form. In the example, 'три' is three, and 'одне́' is 'оди́н', one, in its neuter form, agreeing with the neuter 'сло́во'.

example.target: Ма́ма, ма́ми, ма́мі: одне́ сло́во й три закі́нчення.
example.source_literal: Mom, of-mom, to-mom: one word and three endings.

vocabulary.note: Neuter, because it ends in '-я' after the doubled 'нн', like 'закі́нчення'. The plural has the same form.

example.source: Today it is grammar, and tomorrow a song.

vocabulary.note: Goes directly before the word it negates. The answer 'no' is a different word, 'ні'.

example.source: No, the coffee is not here.

vocabulary.note: At the start of a sentence it is a particle that turns a statement into a yes or no question; English has no word for it, and the literal lines gloss it 'whether'. Between two words it is a conjunction meaning 'or': 'чай чи ка́ва'.
Sets the second statement against what the first leads you to expect. 'А' only sets two statements side by side.

example.source: The coffee is here, but the milk is there.

vocabulary.note: Asks about place. The answer is usually a preposition with a noun in the locative case: 'у шко́лі'.

dialogues.title: Why 'кни́зі'?
dialogues.context: In class, Iryna Petrivna asks Sam where things are on her desk, and Sam notices that 'кни́га' has become 'кни́зі'. To call someone, Ukrainian changes the end of the name (the vocative, note 4): 'Се́ме' is 'Сем' and 'Іри́но Петрі́вно' is 'Іри́на Петрі́вна'. The marks «» are Ukrainian quotation marks. 'Місце́вий' and 'називни́й' are the names of two cases.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.source: The pen is there, in the book.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.source: The key is here, in my hand.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: Yes, the key is in your hand.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Кни́га тут. Але́ ру́чка в кни́зі.
lines.source: The book is here. But the pen is in the book.
lines.source_literal: Book here. But pen in book.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: Так, це місце́вий відмі́нок. Де? У кни́зі, у руці́, у шко́лі.
lines.source: Yes, it is the locative case. Where? In the book, in the hand, at school.
lines.source_literal: Yes, this locative case. Where? In book, in hand, in school.

dialogues.title: Three piles on the table
dialogues.context: Oksana and Taras make a game of sorting the things on the kitchen table into three piles, one for each gender. 'Тара́се' is 'Тара́с' in the vocative. 'Молоко́м' is 'молоко́' in the instrumental case, after 'з', with.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.source: The coffee goes there, and the tea goes here.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.source: And the milk? Here or there?

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Не тут і не там. Це сере́дній рід.
lines.source: Not here and not there. It is neuter.
lines.source_literal: Not here and not there. This middle gender.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.target: Тут. Молоко́, я́блуко й м’я́со тут.
lines.source: Here. The milk, the apple and the meat go here.
lines.source_literal: Here. Milk, apple and meat here.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.source: There! It is coffee, so it is feminine.

dialogues.title: Looking for Oksana
dialogues.context: Sam comes into Andrii's café looking for Oksana, and finds Olena there. 'Андрі́ю' is 'Андрі́й' in the vocative and 'Се́ме' is 'Сем'. 'В університе́ті' is the locative of 'університе́т'; 'в' starts the sentence because a vowel follows.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Тара́с не тут. Тара́с у Льво́ві.
lines.source: Taras is not here. Taras is in Lviv.
lines.source_literal: Taras not here. Taras in Lviv.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.source: The tea is here. And coffee?

grammar.title: Parts of speech and the words of grammar
grammar.explanation:
Grammar describes how words are built and how they combine into sentences. Every later unit uses a small set of names for the kinds of word and for the jobs words do, so this note defines them once, in English and in Ukrainian. Ukrainian teachers and dictionaries use the Ukrainian names.

A part of speech is a class of words that do the same kind of job. Ukrainian grammar counts ten, shown in the table. English grammar has almost the same classes. The one that may be new is the particle, 'ча́стка' (literally 'small part'): a short word that adds a shade of meaning to a word or a whole sentence without naming anything. 'Не' (not) is a particle that negates, and 'чи' is a particle that turns a statement into a yes or no question. English grammar counts 'not' as an adverb; Ukrainian grammar keeps such words in a class of their own.

The ten classes fall into three groups:

- six carry meaning of their own: the noun, adjective, numeral, pronoun, verb and adverb
- three are function words, which link or adjust other words: the preposition, conjunction and particle
- the interjection stands outside the sentence

Words of five classes change their endings: nouns, adjectives, numerals, pronouns and verbs. A few words in these classes have one form only, such as the noun 'кафе́' and the pronoun 'це' in 'Це кни́га'. Prepositions, conjunctions, particles and interjections never change. Adverbs change only to compare, as English 'soon' gives 'sooner', which a later unit teaches.

One spelling can belong to two classes, and its job in the sentence decides. 'Чи' is a particle in 'Чи Окса́на тут?' (is Oksana here?) and a conjunction meaning 'or' in 'чай чи ка́ва' (tea or coffee).

These terms describe the parts of a sentence:

- sentence, 'ре́чення': a complete statement, question or exclamation
- subject, 'підме́т': the person or thing the sentence is about; in 'Ма́ма тут' (mom is here), the subject is 'ма́ма'
- predicate, 'при́судок': what the sentence says about the subject, such as what it does, what it is or where it is; in 'Ма́ма тут', the predicate is 'тут'
- object, 'дода́ток': the person or thing an action is done to; in 'Oksana reads a book', the object is 'a book'

Objects belong mostly to verbs, which the next unit teaches, so nearly every sentence in this unit has only a subject and a predicate.

Beside each natural English translation the course shows a literal line: the Ukrainian words rendered one by one, in Ukrainian order. English words joined by hyphens stand for one Ukrainian word ('of-mom' for 'ма́ми'). The literal line adds no 'a', 'the' or 'is' where Ukrainian has none, so 'Ма́ма тут' is literally 'mom here'.

rows: names a person, place, thing or idea
names a feature of a noun and agrees with it
names a number or a place in an order
stands in for a noun or points at one
names an action or a state; changes for person and time
links a noun to the sentence and decides its case
adds negation, a question or another shade of meaning

examples.source: Oh, the coffee is over there!

grammar.title: No articles, no 'is', and how a sentence is built
grammar.explanation:
English marks nouns with 'a' and 'the' and builds every sentence around a verb. The simplest Ukrainian sentences do neither, which is why the first units could already say 'Ма́ма тут.'

Ukrainian has no articles, the small words 'a', 'an' and 'the'. 'Кни́га' is 'a book' or 'the book', and the English translation adds whichever fits. Ukrainian shows what is known and what is new by word order instead: the known thing comes first and the new information comes last.

- 'Кни́га тут.': the book is already known, and the news is where it is, so English says 'The book is here.'
- 'Тут кни́га.': the place is known, and the news is that there is a book, so English says 'Here is a book.'

In the present tense Ukrainian has no word for 'am', 'is' or 'are'. The verb 'бу́ти', to be, has a single present form, 'є', the same whatever the subject ('I', 'you', 'she' and so on), and Ukrainian uses it to state that something exists: 'Тут є кафе́?' asks 'Is there a café here?'. Elsewhere the place of 'is' stays empty: 'Ма́ма тут.' is literally 'mom here'. 'Це' in 'Це кни́га.' (this is a book) is a pronoun that points at something; it does not mean 'is'.

When both the subject and the predicate are nouns, written Ukrainian puts a dash between them where English has 'is'. A dash cannot be spoken, so this course never writes such a sentence. It says the same thing in one of these ways:

- with a pronoun as the subject: 'Вона́ студе́нтка.' (she is a student)
- with 'це': 'Це Окса́на.' (this is Oksana)
- with negation: 'Окса́на не студе́нтка.' (Oksana is not a student)
- with a verb, once verbs are taught

Word order is free, because the endings of nouns show who does what (note 4). The neutral order is subject, verb, object, as in English. A change of order moves the emphasis, and the word at the end carries the news.

A yes or no question is made in one of two ways:

- the statement said with the voice rising on the word asked about: 'Окса́на тут?'
- 'чи' at the start, which is a little more careful and common in writing: 'Чи Окса́на тут?'

A question with a question word puts that word first: 'Де Окса́на?', 'Хто там?', 'Що це?'.

'Не' (not) goes directly before the word it negates: 'Окса́на не тут.' means 'Oksana is not here'. Placed before another word, it negates that word: 'Тут не Окса́на, а Тара́с.' means 'Taras is here, not Oksana'; after a negated word, 'а' means 'but' or 'but rather'. 'Ні' is the answer 'no', said alone or before a comma: 'Ні, Окса́на там.'

rows: There is a post office there.

grammar.title: Gender, number and agreement
grammar.explanation:
Gender, 'рід', is a class that every Ukrainian noun belongs to. There are three: masculine ('чолові́чий рід'), feminine ('жіно́чий рід') and neuter ('сере́дній рід', literally 'middle gender'). For things, gender is a fact about the word, not about the thing: 'стіл' (table) is masculine, 'кни́га' (book) is feminine and 'вікно́' (window) is neuter, for no reason of meaning. English keeps a trace of gender only in 'he', 'she' and 'it'. Gender matters because the adjectives, the pronouns and some of the numerals attached to a noun take their form from the noun's gender.

A word that changes has two parts. The ending, 'закі́нчення', is the part at the end that changes from form to form; the stem is the part before it, which stays and carries the meaning. In 'кни́га' and 'кни́ги' (books), the stem is 'книг-' and the endings are '-а' and '-и'. The dictionary form is the form a dictionary lists a word under; for a noun it is the singular form that names the subject. Some dictionary forms, such as 'брат', end in their stem, with no ending at all.

The ending of the dictionary form tells the gender of most nouns, as the table shows:

- masculine: a consonant ('брат'), '-й' ('чай') or '-ь' ('день')
- feminine: '-а' ('ма́ма') or '-я' ('земля́')
- neuter: '-о' ('вікно́'), '-е' ('мо́ре', sea), or '-я' after a doubled consonant ('життя́', 'ре́чення')

Three groups need care:

- nouns in '-ь' can be masculine ('день', 'оліве́ць') or feminine ('сіль', 'о́сінь'), so learn each one with its gender
- 'ім’я́' (first name) is neuter although it ends in '-я' with no doubled consonant, while 'сім’я́' (family) follows the rule and is feminine; some other neuter nouns in '-я' behave like 'ім’я́'
- most borrowed nouns that name things, end in a vowel and never change their form, such as 'кафе́', are neuter

Natural gender, the sex of the person a noun names, wins over the ending. A noun that can name only a man is masculine whatever its ending: 'та́то' (dad) ends in '-о' and 'Мико́ла' in '-а', but both are masculine, and every word that agrees with them takes the masculine form.

Number is singular, 'одни́на', or plural, 'множина́'. English adds '-s'; Ukrainian replaces the ending. In the nominative, the case of the dictionary form (note 4), the plural of most nouns ends in one of three ways:

- '-и' for most masculine and feminine nouns whose last consonant is hard: 'кни́га', 'кни́ги'; 'брат', 'брати́'
- '-і' for most masculine and feminine nouns whose last consonant is soft or is 'ж', 'ч', 'ш' or 'щ': 'земля́', 'зе́млі'; 'день', 'дні'; 'ключ', 'ключі́'
- '-а' for neuter nouns in '-о': 'мі́сто', 'міста́'; 'вікно́', 'ві́кна'

Neuter nouns such as 'ре́чення' and 'закі́нчення' have the same form in both numbers. As the unit on stress showed, the stress often moves in the plural, so learn each plural with its stress. These forms are a preview; a later unit teaches the plural in full.

Agreement is the rule that a word attached to a noun copies the noun's gender, number and case. An adjective shows it in its ending. The adjective 'нови́й' (new) has these forms in the nominative:

- masculine: 'нови́й стіл' (a new table)
- feminine: 'нова́ кни́га' (a new book)
- neuter: 'нове́ вікно́' (a new window)
- plural, the same for every gender: 'нові́ кни́ги' (new books)

Adjectives whose stem ends in a soft consonant, such as 'сере́дній' (middle), have '-ій', '-я' and '-є' in place of '-ий', '-а' and '-е', and the same plural '-і': 'сере́дній', 'сере́дня', 'сере́днє', 'сере́дні'. The names of the genders are themselves adjectives agreeing with the masculine noun 'рід': 'чолові́чий рід', 'жіно́чий рід', 'сере́дній рід'. Agreement also covers case: in 'у нові́й кни́зі' (in the new book) both words are in the locative case (note 4). An English adjective keeps one form for every noun; a Ukrainian adjective changes with the noun it describes.

examples.target: Тут нова́ ру́чка, а там нови́й оліве́ць.
examples.source: Here is a new pen, and there is a new pencil.
examples.source_literal: Here new pen, and there new pencil.

examples.source: The pen is in the new book.

grammar.title: Cases: what endings do
grammar.explanation:
A case is a form of a noun that shows the noun's job in the sentence. English does almost all of this with word order and prepositions: 'Oksana sees Taras' and 'Taras sees Oksana' have the same words, and only their order says who sees whom. English keeps cases in a few pronouns: 'he' sees, someone sees 'him', and a book is 'his'.

Ukrainian gives nouns, adjectives, numerals and pronouns sets of case forms, made with endings. The ending, not the position, shows the job. In 'Окса́на ба́чить Тара́са' ('ба́чить' means 'sees'), the ending '-а' added to 'Тара́с' marks him as the one seen. So 'Тара́са ба́чить Окса́на' still means that Oksana sees Taras; the new order only moves the emphasis onto Oksana. This is why Ukrainian word order is free.

Ukrainian has seven cases, 'відмі́нки'. Ukrainian children learn them at school with one or two question words each, and the questions are a useful test: the form that answers 'хто?' or 'що?' (who? what?) is the nominative, the form that answers 'кого́?' or 'чого́?' (of whom? of what?) is the genitive, and so on. 'Кого́?' belongs to two cases, the genitive and the accusative, so each case is recognized by its pair of questions. The table gives each case with its Ukrainian name, its questions, its main job and the form of 'ма́ма' (mom) it takes. The locative is never used without a preposition, so its questions include one, 'на' (on, at).

Each preposition takes a particular case, and some take different cases for different meanings:

- 'у' or 'в' with the locative means 'in' or 'at': 'у шко́лі' (at school), 'в Украї́ні' (in Ukraine)
- 'з' with the genitive means 'from': 'з Ки́єва' (from Kyiv), 'зі шко́ли' (from school)
- 'з' with the instrumental means 'with': 'ка́ва з молоко́м' (coffee with milk), 'чай із цу́кром' (tea with sugar)

These are the phrases met whole in the unit on stress, and the changed endings in them are case endings.

The endings also depend on the noun's gender and number, so one noun can have up to fourteen forms, though many of them look alike. Nobody learns them all at once. The course takes the cases in this order:

- the nominative and the vocative
- the accusative, for the object of a verb
- the locative, for where things are
- the genitive, for possession, absence and 'from'
- the dative and the instrumental, at level A2; before that they appear only in fixed phrases such as 'ка́ва з молоко́м'

The vocative is the form for calling or addressing someone, and Ukrainian uses it in everyday speech. 'Ма́ма' becomes 'ма́мо', 'Окса́на' becomes 'Окса́но', 'Сем' becomes 'Се́ме' and 'Андрі́й' becomes 'Андрі́ю'. A later unit gives the rules for making it.

rows: the object of an action; direction after 'у'
where something is; only after a preposition

examples.source: The coffee is for mom, and the juice is for dad.

grammar.title: Sounds that change inside a word
grammar.explanation:
An alternation is a regular change of one sound, and so one letter, into another inside a word when its form changes. Ukrainian has a few that appear as soon as an ending is added, so you will meet them in almost every unit. They are why a vocabulary note sometimes gives a stem that differs from the dictionary form, as with 'дім' and the stem 'дом-'.

The first depends on the syllable. An open syllable ends in a vowel; a closed syllable ends in a consonant. In 'ко-та́', a form of 'кіт' (cat), the 'о' ends its syllable, which is open. In 'кіт' the 'т' follows in the same syllable, which is closed. Many words have 'о' or 'е' in an open syllable and 'і' in the same place when that syllable is closed, which usually happens in the dictionary form, the one with no ending:

- 'кіт', other forms 'кота́', 'коти́'
- 'стіл', 'столи́' (tables)
- 'дім', 'у до́мі' (in the house)
- 'ніс', 'но́са' (of the nose)
- 'рід', 'ро́ду' (of the gender)
- 'Львів', 'у Льво́ві' (in Lviv)
- 'о́сінь', 'о́сені' (of autumn), with 'е'

After a vowel the same change turns 'є' into 'ї': 'Ки́їв', 'з Ки́єва', 'у Ки́єві'.

The change happened long ago in the sound of the language, and the spelling follows the sound. It cannot be run backwards, because many words have an 'і' that never changes: 'хліб' keeps it in 'хлі́ба' (of the bread). A dictionary form with 'і' does not tell you whether other forms have 'о' or 'е', so the vocabulary notes say so when they do.

The second change is a vowel that drops out. Some words lose the 'о' or 'е' of their last syllable when an ending is added: 'цу́кор' (sugar) gives 'чай із цу́кром', 'оліве́ць' (pencil) gives 'олівця́' (of the pencil), and 'день' (day) gives 'дні' (days).

The third concerns the consonants 'г', 'к' and 'х'. Before the ending '-і', which feminine nouns take in the locative and the dative, they become 'з', 'ц' and 'с':

- 'кни́га', 'у кни́зі' (in the book)
- 'рука́', 'у руці́' (in the hand)
- 'нога́', 'на нозі́' (on the foot)
- 'жі́нка', 'жі́нці' (to the woman)
- 'му́ха' (fly, the insect), 'на му́сі' (on a fly)

This change goes back to an old sound law of the language; today it is a fixed rule of both speech and spelling. The table sums up the three changes.

examples.source: The table is here, and the tables are there.
The cat is in the house.

examples.target: Хліб із Ки́єва, а сир із Льво́ва.
examples.source: The bread is from Kyiv, and the cheese is from Lviv.
examples.source_literal: Bread from Kyiv, and cheese from Lviv.

examples.target: Тут цу́кор, а там чай із цу́кром.
examples.source: Here is the sugar, and there is tea with sugar.
examples.source_literal: Here sugar, and there tea with sugar.

examples.source: The pen is in my hand.

culture.title: Grammar at school and the Day of Ukrainian Writing and Language
culture.text:
Ukrainian children learn the seven cases at primary school by reciting each one with its questions: 'називни́й: хто? що?', 'родови́й: кого́? чого́?', and so on to the vocative. Adults still remember the list, and asking the case question is how many Ukrainians check a form they are unsure of.

The Ukrainian names of grammar are built from Ukrainian words, while English 'noun' and 'pronoun' come from Latin. A Ukrainian speaker therefore hears what each term means:

- 'іме́нник' (noun) is built on 'ім’я́', name
- 'займе́нник' (pronoun) is built on 'ім’я́' too: a word that stands in for a name
- 'дієсло́во' (verb) joins 'ді́я', action, and 'сло́во', word
- 'числі́вник' (numeral) is built on 'число́', number
- 'відмі́нок' (case) is built on 'відміня́ти', to change

Every year on 9 November Ukraine marks the Day of Ukrainian Writing and Language. Schools, universities and offices hold events, and national radio broadcasts a dictation, a text read aloud slowly for listeners to write down. People across the country write it at the same moment and then check their spelling against the published text; getting every ending and every apostrophe right is a matter of pride.

The rules of spelling are set out in 'Украї́нський правопи́с', the official spelling code, revised in 2019. This course follows the 2019 rules.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian word of grammar with its English meaning
exercises.explanation: 'Іме́нник', 'займе́нник' and 'прийме́нник' are all built on 'ім’я́', name.

exercises.prompt: In 'Чай тут, а ка́ва там.', which word is a conjunction?
exercises.explanation: 'А' joins two statements that are set side by side. 'Чай' is a noun, and 'тут' and 'там' are adverbs.

exercises.prompt: How does Ukrainian tell 'a book' from 'the book'?
choices: With a different ending for 'the book'
It does not: 'кни́га' is used for both
With 'це' before the word for 'the book'
exercises.explanation: Ukrainian has no articles. Context and word order show which is meant: the known thing comes first and new information last.
'Не' stands before 'там', the word it negates.

exercises.hint_source: No, the juice is not here.
exercises.explanation: 'Ні' answers 'no'; 'не' means 'not' and goes directly before the word it negates.
'Чи' at the start turns a statement into a yes or no question.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'Here is a book', with the book as the new information?
exercises.explanation: New information comes last. 'Кни́га тут.' treats the book as known and says where it is.

choices: There is a post office here.
There is a post office there.
exercises.explanation: 'Є' states that something exists; 'там' is 'there' and 'по́шта' is the post office.

exercises.prompt: Which of these nouns is masculine?
exercises.explanation: 'Та́то' ends in '-о' but names a man, and natural gender wins over the ending. The others are neuter nouns in '-о'.

choices: It names a thing, not a person
It ends in '-я' after a doubled consonant
exercises.explanation: Nouns in '-я' after a doubled consonant are neuter. A noun in '-я' such as 'земля́' is feminine.
'Вода́' ends in '-а' and 'пі́сня' in '-я'; 'о́сінь' is one of the feminine nouns in '-ь'. 'Жіно́чий' agrees with the masculine noun 'рід'.

exercises.hint_source: This is a new book. (dictionary form: 'нови́й')
exercises.explanation: 'Кни́га' is feminine singular, so the adjective ends in '-а'.

exercises.hint_source: Here is a new window. (dictionary form: 'нови́й')
exercises.explanation: 'Вікно́' is neuter singular, so the adjective ends in '-е'.
Neuter nouns in '-о' take '-а' in the plural, and here the stress moves to the ending.
'Не' goes directly before 'тут'; Ukrainian has no word for 'is' here.
'Чи' opens the question and the rest keeps the order of the statement.

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, why does Taras put 'ка́ва з молоко́м' with the feminine nouns?
choices: 'Ка́ва' is feminine, and it decides the gender of the phrase
exercises.explanation: The main noun of the phrase is 'ка́ва'. 'Молоко́м' is the neuter noun 'молоко́' in the instrumental case after 'з'.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian name of each case with its English name
exercises.explanation: The seventh case is the vocative, 'кли́чний'.

exercises.prompt: Which case answers the questions 'хто?' and 'що?'?
exercises.explanation: The nominative, 'називни́й', names the subject and is the dictionary form.

exercises.prompt: In the café, why does Sam say 'Андрі́ю' and not 'Андрі́й'?
choices: 'Андрі́ю' shows that Andrii is the subject
He is calling Andrii, so he uses the vocative
exercises.explanation: The vocative, 'кли́чний', is the form for calling or addressing someone.

choices: The pen is in the book.
The pen is in the hand.
The key is in the book.
exercises.explanation: 'Кни́зі' is 'кни́га' in the locative after 'в'.

exercises.hint_source: The pen is in my hand. (dictionary form: 'рука́')
exercises.explanation: The locative ending '-і' turns the 'к' of 'рука́' into 'ц'.

exercises.hint_source: The key is in the book. (dictionary form: 'кни́га')
exercises.explanation: The locative ending '-і' turns the 'г' of 'кни́га' into 'з'.

exercises.prompt: 'Кіт' has the other form 'кота́'. Why does the dictionary form have 'і'?
exercises.explanation: In 'ко-та́' the 'о' ends an open syllable. In 'кіт' the syllable is closed by 'т', and the old 'о' is said and written 'і'.
The adjective agrees with the feminine noun 'кни́га', and the new information comes last.
The question word comes first, and there is no word for 'is' or 'the'.
'Стіл' is masculine, so the adjective is 'нови́й'. 'Це' points; it does not mean 'is'.

exercises.prompt_source: Oksana is here, but Taras is there.
exercises.explanation: Either 'а' or 'але́' joins the two contrasting statements.

exercises.hint_source: The coffee with milk is here.
The bread is here, and the cheese is there.
